1.title: A surface code patch
1.intro: Nine physical qubits in a 3 by 3 grid hold one logical qubit. An encoder spreads |0> over all nine, and eight checks (four X, four Z) watch for errors. Pick an error next to the Play button to see which checks fire.
shows: The patch is nine data qubits in a 3 by 3 grid, watched by eight checks: four X and four Z. The encoder takes eight steps. Two CNOTs copy q0 along the top row, H makes q4, q5, q6 and q7 the sources of the X checks, and their CNOTs fan out until all eight checks hold and the patch is |0>_L.

An injected error strikes right after encoding. An X error fires the Z checks that share its qubit, a Z error fires the X checks, and a Y error fires both. The page looks the Z syndrome up in a table of single errors and applies X to the qubit it names. A Z error cannot change a Z readout, so here it is harmless.
try: Pick X on q4 in the Inject an error menu and press Play. Two Z checks fire, and the table points back at q4.
Pick X on q6. Only one Z check fires and the table applies X to q3 instead; X on q3 and q6 is itself an X check, so nothing logical changes.
Pick Z on q4: two X checks fire and the Z readout stays correct.
Drag the slider, or click a block in the strip, to stop on any step.
1.plain: A real quantum code has to catch two kinds of error, bit flips and phase flips. This page builds the smallest surface code: nine qubits in a square that together hold one protected qubit, watched by eight checks. You can strike any qubit with an error and see which checks notice it.
results_note: Every shot ends with all data qubits measured, and the checks are worked out from those bits. Clean shots only gives the rate over the shots in which no check fired. Corrected by the code is the share of shots in which checks fired and a table of single errors named a qubit to flip back; After correction is the rate over all kept shots once that flip is made. Discarded by the checks is the share of shots whose fired checks are not in the table at all: those shots are dropped. No correction reads the raw bits of every shot. Bare qubits runs the same logical circuit with one unprotected qubit in place of each patch: no encoder and no checks. Each rate comes with one binomial standard error.

Why the code loses here: the noise in this simulation acts only on gates, as the line under the table says. The bare row reads a qubit left in |0> with no gate acting on it, so no noise reaches it: it is a trivial control, not a fair rival. The patch goes through the twelve CNOTs of the encoder, and one faulty CNOT can leave errors on two qubits that the table of single errors then completes into a logical flip. The encoder is not fault tolerant: in the course's own stabilizer simulator, 44 of the 180 ways a single CNOT of the lesson 1 encoder can fail (each of its 12 CNOTs followed by one of the 15 two-qubit Pauli errors) end in a wrong logical readout after the table's correction.

2.title: Logical CNOT between two patches
2.intro: Both patches use the encoder from lesson 1: A becomes |+>_L, B becomes |0>_L. Nine physical CNOTs, one between each pair of matching qubits, then act as one logical CNOT and leave a logical Bell pair.
shows: Patch A is encoded as |+>_L and patch B as |0>_L, both with the encoder from lesson 1. Nine CNOTs, one from each qubit of A to the matching qubit of B, then act as one logical CNOT. Each copies X forward and Z backward, so X_L of A becomes X_L of A times X_L of B, and Z_L of B becomes Z_L of A times Z_L of B. Checks map to checks, so all sixteen still hold, and one faulty CNOT hits each patch at most once. The result is a logical Bell pair: read in Z, the two logical bits come out random but always equal.
try: Press Play and follow the state panel under the figure: A becomes |+>_L, B becomes |0>_L, and after the CNOT layer both are listed as a Bell pair.

In Run it live, set the shots, the readout basis and the noise per gate, then press Run. A stabilizer simulator runs the circuit in your browser and reports how often the two logical bits agree and how many shots the checks discard.
Tick Inject one error, choose a Pauli, a qubit and the layer it follows, and run again. The heatmap shows how often each of the sixteen checks fired in each layer.
2.plain: To compute, protected qubits have to act on each other. Here two patches of nine qubits are joined by nine ordinary CNOT gates, one per matching pair, and together these act as one CNOT on the two protected qubits. The result is a Bell pair: two protected qubits whose readouts in Z always agree.
results_note: Every shot ends with all data qubits measured, and the checks are worked out from those bits. Clean shots only gives the rate over the shots in which no check fired. Corrected by the code is the share of shots in which checks fired and a table of single errors named a qubit to flip back; After correction is the rate over all kept shots once that flip is made. Discarded by the checks is the share of shots whose fired checks are not in the table at all: those shots are dropped. No correction reads the raw bits of every shot. Bare qubits runs the same logical circuit with one unprotected qubit in place of each patch: no encoder and no checks. Each rate comes with one binomial standard error.
The first row reads a single patch prepared as |+>_L in X, with no CNOT: the starting state of patch A, kept as a reference for the two-patch rows.

Why the code loses here: the noise in this simulation acts only on gates, as the line under the table says. Both patches come from the lesson 1 encoder, and the two-patch rows add the nine transversal CNOTs on top. The bare rows use one qubit per patch and none of those CNOTs, so far less noise reaches them. The encoder is not fault tolerant: in the course's own stabilizer simulator, 44 of the 180 ways a single CNOT of the lesson 1 encoder can fail (each of its 12 CNOTs followed by one of the 15 two-qubit Pauli errors) end in a wrong logical readout after the table's correction.

3.title: Preparing a T state
3.intro: H and T on q0 make the T state on one physical qubit; the encoder from lesson 1 carries it over as |T>_L. It is read in X (and Y): ideally 1 comes up in 14.6% of shots.
shows: H and then T on q0 make the T state on one physical qubit. The lesson 1 encoder carries it into the patch as |T>_L. Neither X_L nor Z_L holds now, because the T state is an eigenstate of neither. To read X_L, H on all nine qubits swaps X and Z: the checks swap type and all eight still hold. Measuring every qubit in Z then gives X_L, which ideally reads 1 in 14.6% of shots. Lesson 4 teleports this state to another patch.
try: Step with the arrow keys on the slider and watch the state panel go from q0 = |+> to q0 = T|+> to |T>_L.
Stop on the step H on A, the readout rotation: the checks swap type and all eight still hold.

In the Simulated results table, compare the X and Y rows. Both have the ideal 14.6%; the other columns come from a noisy simulation in Qiskit Aer. A patch read in Y has no checks to read, so its check columns show n/a.
3.plain: This page prepares a T state, a particular one-qubit state that lesson 4 uses, on a single qubit and then carries it into a nine-qubit patch. Read in X many times, it should give 1 in about 14.6% of shots, and the table compares simulated runs with that number.
results_note: Every shot ends with all data qubits measured, and the checks are worked out from those bits. Clean shots only gives the rate over the shots in which no check fired. Corrected by the code is the share of shots in which checks fired and a table of single errors named a qubit to flip back; After correction is the rate over all kept shots once that flip is made. Discarded by the checks is the share of shots whose fired checks are not in the table at all: those shots are dropped. No correction reads the raw bits of every shot. Bare qubits runs the same logical circuit with one unprotected qubit in place of each patch: no encoder and no checks. Each rate comes with one binomial standard error.

A patch read in Y has no checks to read, so its row gets no correction: After correction equals No correction, and the check columns show n/a. The bare rows prepare the T state on one qubit with no encoder and land within about one standard error of the ideal 14.6%. The encoded X row does too; the encoded Y row, with nothing to correct it, is the furthest from the ideal. The encoder is the one from lesson 1, which a single faulty CNOT can defeat.

4.title: Teleporting the T state
4.intro: Patch A holds |T>_L (lesson 3), B and C become a logical Bell pair (lesson 2), then a logical CNOT A to B and the readouts of A in X and B in Z teleport the T state to C, up to a Pauli fix applied to the measured bits.
shows: Patch A holds |T>_L, prepared as in lesson 3. Patches B and C become a logical Bell pair through the logical CNOT of lesson 2. A logical CNOT from A to B then ties the T state to the pair. A is read in X and B in Z, and those two bits say which Pauli fix C needs. C is read in X as well, to check that it now holds the T state. The ideal logical circuit on the page draws the same protocol, with X to the power M2 and Z to the power M1 applied to C.
try: Click the two transversal CNOT blocks in the strip, B to C and then A to B, to see nine gates between matching qubits in each.
Stop just after the CNOT from A to B: the state panel lists all three patches as entangled with the other patches.
The Simulated results table reports C read in X and in Y after the Pauli fix, from a noisy simulation in Qiskit Aer, next to the ideal 14.6%.
4.plain: Teleportation moves a qubit's state onto another qubit using a shared Bell pair and two measured bits, without sending the qubit itself. Here the T state from lesson 3 is teleported from one nine-qubit patch to another, and the two measured bits decide which fix is applied to the result.
results_note: Every shot ends with all data qubits measured, and the checks are worked out from those bits. Clean shots only gives the rate over the shots in which no check fired. Corrected by the code is the share of shots in which checks fired and a table of single errors named a qubit to flip back; After correction is the rate over all kept shots once that flip is made. Discarded by the checks is the share of shots whose fired checks are not in the table at all: those shots are dropped. No correction reads the raw bits of every shot. Bare qubits runs the same logical circuit with one unprotected qubit in place of each patch: no encoder and no checks. Each rate comes with one binomial standard error.
C read in Y has no checks of its own, but A and B are still corrected, and their bits set the Pauli fix, so the Y row has correction columns too.

Why the code loses here: the noise in this simulation acts only on gates, as the line under the table says. Teleportation runs three encoders and two transversal CNOTs, against a handful of gates for the bare qubits. In the Y row, After correction (25.9%) and No correction (25.2%) differ by less than one standard error: with an encoder that one fault can defeat, the table's corrections do not reliably help. The encoder is not fault tolerant: in the course's own stabilizer simulator, 44 of the 180 ways a single CNOT of the lesson 1 encoder can fail (each of its 12 CNOTs followed by one of the 15 two-qubit Pauli errors) end in a wrong logical readout after the table's correction.
